# Two Years On: Follow-up of the Varden County Trial and a Subset of Halden Pilot Organisations

*Field report. A. Lindqvist, P. Mahony, D. Rao (Varden County Evaluation Unit / Easterly University) and R. Okafor (Halden Institute for Work Studies). Registered follow-up protocol VC-2023-04-F, filed at month 11.*

## Summary

We report 24-month outcomes from two sources: the Varden County cluster-randomised trial, whose case-processing offices remained on their assigned schedules for two years, and 14 organisations from the Halden pilot that hold record-based output data. In Varden case-processing offices, the gain in output per actual hour relative to control fell from 12.5% at nine months to 8.5% at 24 months, measured with system log data, and output per employee stood at −3.4% (95% CI −8.0 to +1.2). The gain has therefore declined but not disappeared. A registered mediation test confirms that the reduction in recurring meetings accounts for 47% (95% CI 28 to 66%) of the per-hour gain; improved fatigue accounts for 18% (2 to 34%). The counter and contact-centre arm was ended by the county at month 12 because of waiting times. Three of the 14 Halden organisations have reverted, all with client-facing or coverage obligations.

## 1. Background

The nine-month report of the Varden trial left three questions to be settled at follow-up: whether the per-hour gain in case-processing would persist; whether the meetings association, found in an unregistered analysis, would survive a registered test; and whether timesheets understated the work actually done. Two subsequent publications bear on the first two. A re-analysis of the Halden pilot argued that per-hour gains in reduced-hours schemes are entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty, and that the meetings hypothesis was a post hoc story. A meta-analysis of 23 studies concluded that effects show no sign of decay, on the basis of four studies with follow-up beyond 12 months. We address each directly.

## 2. Varden County: design at 24 months

The seven treated and seven control case-processing offices kept their assigned schedules for 24 months. To address concern about unrecorded work, we added a second hours measure: active log-in time on the county's case-management system, which records time staff are working on cases whether or not they claim it on a timesheet. The mediation analysis was registered at month 11, before 24-month outcomes were available. It specified two mediators, weekly hours in recurring meetings (from calendar data) and a validated fatigue scale, and a single outcome, output per log-measured hour.

The counter and contact-centre arm was ended by the county at month 12. In months 10 to 12, average waiting time in treated counter offices was 7.3 minutes against 4.0 in control offices, and the county judged that restoring service would require 12% more staff, raising the cost per contact handled by an estimated 9%. Those offices returned to 37.5 hours.

## 3. Varden County: results

**Table 1. Case-processing offices, treated relative to control (difference-in-differences)**

| Outcome | 9 months | 24 months |
|---|---|---|
| Output per FTE | −2.1% (−6.8 to +2.6) | −3.4% (−8.0 to +1.2) |
| Actual hours, timesheets | −13% | −12% |
| Actual hours, system logs | — | −11% |
| Output per hour, timesheets | +12.5% (+6.9 to +18.4) | +9.8% (+4.6 to +15.2) |
| Output per hour, system logs | — | +8.5% (+3.4 to +13.8) |
| Appeal overturn rate (treated v control) | 3.1% v 3.0% | 3.2% v 3.0% |
| Sick days per FTE | −29% | −27% |
| Annual resignations (treated v control) | 3.9% v 7.4% | 4.1% v 7.9% |

Log data show slightly more work than timesheets: actual hours fell by 11% on logs and 12% on timesheets, so the per-hour gain on the stricter measure is 8.5%. That gain is smaller than at nine months but its confidence interval excludes zero by a clear margin. Output per employee remains slightly below control; the hours reduction is mostly, not fully, offset.

The decline from 12.5% to 9.8% on the like-for-like timesheet measure is consistent with some fading of an initial effect. It is not consistent with the gain falling to zero by month ten, as an extrapolation of self-reported energy in the Halden data had suggested.

### Mediation

Recurring meeting time in treated case-processing offices fell from 7.4 to 3.9 hours per week per person between baseline and month 24; in control offices it moved from 7.2 to 7.0. Fatigue scores improved by 0.34 standard deviations in treated offices relative to control.

**Table 2. Registered mediation analysis, output per log-measured hour, 24 months**

| Pathway | Share of per-hour gain explained (95% CI) |
|---|---|
| Reduction in recurring meetings | 47% (28 to 66) |
| Improvement in fatigue | 18% (2 to 34) |
| Unexplained | 35% |

The meetings pathway, first suggested in the nine-month report's exploratory analysis and since dismissed as post hoc, survives a registered test with a larger sample of office-months and a pre-specified model. Reduced fatigue contributes, but less than half as much. About a third of the gain is not explained by either measured pathway.

### An unplanned observation

In month 15, two control offices, on their own initiative and without changing hours, carried out a "meeting audit" and cancelled a number of standing meetings. Recurring meeting time in those two offices fell from 7.1 to 5.0 hours per week, and their output per hour over the following six months was 4.1% above their own previous six months. This is two offices, uncontrolled, and the change was smaller than in treated offices. It suggests, without establishing, that part of the per-hour gain might be available without reducing hours. Whether reorganisation alone could capture most of the gain, or whether the hours cut is what makes such reorganisation happen and stick, cannot be determined from this trial, since no arm reorganised without reducing hours.

## 4. Halden organisations at 24 months

We contacted the 23 Halden organisations that had submitted output records; 14 agreed to provide 24-month data. Three of these had reverted to a five-day schedule: a hospitality group and a retail chain, both citing coverage of opening hours, and a marketing agency citing client deadlines. Their record-based output indices at the time of reversion were between 88 and 91.

Among the 11 that continued, record-based output at 24 months stood at 96.8 against the pre-pilot baseline, and actual hours from time tracking at 34.9 against 40.3 (−13.4%), an implied gain in output per actual hour of 11.8%. These organisations have no comparison group and are survivors twice over: they completed the pilot and then chose to continue. Their figures are an upper bound for organisations that self-select into reduced hours and find it suits them, not an estimate for organisations in general.

## 5. Bearing on earlier claims

**The re-analysis's claim that per-hour gains are entirely an artifact.** The Varden 24-month estimate uses record-based output, log-measured hours, randomised comparison and a two-year horizon, the standards that re-analysis itself recommended, and finds a gain of 8.5% (3.4 to 13.8). The re-analysis was right about the measurement problems it identified and right that headline figures were inflated; its conclusion that nothing remains once those problems are corrected is not supported.

**The meta-analysis's claim that effects show no sign of decay.** The four studies with follow-up beyond 12 months, listed in the meta-analysis's supplementary table, were all uncontrolled and all used scheduled hours. Their pooled estimate therefore reflects the design features the meta-analysis itself found to inflate effects, and it cannot speak to decay. In the one controlled study with long follow-up, this one, the per-hour gain declined by about a quarter between nine and 24 months.

## 6. Limitations

One public employer; seven offices per arm in the case-processing stratum. Mediation analysis assumes no unmeasured confounding between mediators and outcome, which a cluster trial cannot guarantee. The Halden subset is small and self-selected. Neither source extends beyond 24 months.

response:
# Review: Two-Year Follow-up of Varden County and Halden Organisations

This report directly addresses the open questions from the earlier papers:
- It adds a second hours measure that captures unclaimed work.
- It registers the mediation test before the 24-month outcomes were available.
- It reports the counter arm's termination candidly.
- It shows that the meta-analysis's "no decay" claim rested on four uncontrolled, scheduled-hours studies.

Its adjudication of the earlier claims is mostly fair. The re-analysis was right about the measurement problems but wrong that nothing remains. The meta-analysis's duration evidence couldn't support its conclusion.

**The core figures check out:**
- 0.966 / 0.88 = +9.8% per hour on timesheets
- 0.966 / 0.89 = +8.5% per hour on logs
- Halden: 96.8 / 0.866 = +11.8%, and 34.9 / 40.3 = −13.4%

There are, however, several internal inconsistencies and some overstated claims, especially about the mediation result.

## 1. The two control offices' meeting audit contaminated the control group

From month 15, two of the seven control offices cut their meetings and saw output per hour rise by about 4%. This matters in three ways.

- **It reduces the 24-month estimate.** If two of seven controls improved by about 4%, the control average rose by roughly 1.2 points. That alone could account for close to half of the 2.7-point fall from 12.5% to 9.8%. Part of the apparent fading may be improvement in the controls, not decline in the treated offices. Report the treated and control series separately over time, and re-estimate without the two audited offices as a sensitivity check.
- **It doesn't match the control meeting average.** Two offices falling by 2.1 hours each would lower the seven-office average by about 0.6 hours, from 7.2 to about 6.6. The report says control meetings moved from 7.2 to 7.0, so the other five offices must have risen by about 0.56 hours each. That may be true, but it needs to be stated.
- **The 4.1% figure has no comparison.** It compares those offices with their own previous six months, without seasonal adjustment or a comparison group. A difference-in-differences against the other five control offices would be easy to compute.

## 2. The headline compares two different measures

The summary says the gain "fell from 12.5% at nine months to 8.5% at 24 months". But 12.5% is a timesheet figure and 8.5% is a log figure.

| Comparison | Decline |
|---|---|
| Timesheets 12.5% → timesheets 9.8% (like-for-like) | about a fifth (−22%) |
| Timesheets 12.5% → logs 8.5% (mixed) | about a third (−32%) |

Section 5's "declined by about a quarter" matches neither figure. The summary should report the like-for-like decline, then note separately that the stricter log measure gives 8.5%.

## 3. What the log measure counts affects the mediation result

"Active log-in time on the case-management system" measures time spent in the case system. It is not total work time. This matters for two reasons.

- **It is not simply a stricter measure.** Logs miss meetings, phone calls, training and offline work. Calling the log figure "stricter" assumes it captures everything timesheets do and more. Report the hours *levels* under both measures, not just the percentage changes.
- **It changes what the meetings mediation can mean.** If meeting time is not in the log denominator, simply removing meetings shifts time into case work. That raises output and logged hours together, leaving output per logged hour unchanged. For meetings to explain 47% of the gain in output per *logged* hour, they must work through another channel: fragmented attention, interruptions, or staff logged in during meetings. Whichever it is, the report should say which, because "removing low-value time" and "reducing fragmentation" are different mechanisms with different implications for other employers.

## 4. The mediation is better described as "supported" than "confirmed"

- **Same units as the exploratory finding.** Registering the test before the 24-month outcomes prevents analytic flexibility. But the test uses the same seven treated offices that generated the hypothesis, and some of the mediator data (months 1–11) were already observed when the test was registered. This is stronger than the original correlation, but it is not an independent replication.
- **Effective sample size.** "A larger sample of office-months" adds observations, but there are still only 14 clusters. Were standard errors clustered by office in the mediation model? A 95% CI of 28–66% looks narrow for 14 clusters.
- **Identification.** Mediators are not randomised. The Limitations section acknowledges this, but the Summary says the test "confirms" the result. Use "supports" or "is consistent with".
- **Additive decomposition.** Presenting the shares as 47% + 18% + 35% unexplained assumes the two pathways don't interact. Meetings and fatigue are plausibly linked, since fewer meetings could reduce fatigue. Report how the mediators were modelled together.
- **Baseline meeting data.** The nine-month report said calendar data were collected only in month six. This report gives baseline figures (7.4 treated, 7.2 control). Where did they come from: retrieved calendar histories? State the method.

## 5. Retention may account for part of the unexplained 35%

Annual resignations are about 4% in treated offices against 8% in control. Over two years, control offices will have more new and less experienced staff, which lowers their output per hour. This is a genuine effect of the treatment, but through **staff composition** rather than meetings or fatigue. It may be part of the unexplained 35%. Adjusting for tenure, or analysing only staff present throughout, would test this.

## 6. Counter arm: the cost figure needs its working

"Restoring service would require 12% more staff, raising the cost per contact handled by an estimated 9%." With roughly fixed demand and new staff on the same pay, 12% more staff to serve the same contacts implies about **+12%** cost per contact relative to the pre-trial baseline. Compared with the trial period, when contacts had already fallen, the change would be close to zero. Neither comparison gives 9%. Please give the calculation and the baseline: lower pay for new hires, recovered demand, or something else.

## 7. Halden subset

- **Baseline mismatch.** The 40.3-hour baseline equals the 27-organisation figure from the re-analysis. The 11 continuing organisations need their own baseline. Do all 11 have time tracking? Only 17 of the 23 with records did.
- **"Upper bound" is not guaranteed.** Self-selection pushes the estimate up. But with no comparison group, changes over 2.5 years (new software and AI tools, labour-market shifts, client mix) could push it in either direction. Call it "an estimate for self-selected continuers, likely biased upward by selection", not a strict upper bound.
- **Non-response.** 9 of the 23 organisations declined. Report any known characteristics of those that declined, such as sector and pilot-period output, and any information on whether they reverted.
- **Reverted organisations.** The three reversions (output indices 88–91, all with coverage or client-deadline obligations) usefully extend the work-type finding. A marketing agency citing client deadlines suggests some "discretionary" work has hidden coverage constraints.

## 8. Smaller points

- **Sick days** are still counted per FTE in days. The earlier concern applies: a four-day schedule mechanically reduces sick days. Report sick hours as a share of scheduled hours.
- **Quality** (3.2% v 3.0%) has no CI. A 24-month window better captures appeal lags, which is good, but give the interval.
- **"Not consistent with falling to zero by month ten".** That extrapolation was about Halden, not Varden. The Varden data refute it for Varden. The 11 Halden continuers are consistent with a persistent gain but uncontrolled. Say so precisely.
- **Conflicts of interest.** R. Okafor co-authored the Halden working paper, and the Varden authors are evaluating criticism of their own exploratory analysis. Neither is improper, but declare both. An independent re-analysis of the registered mediation would strengthen the conclusions.
- **Tone.** "Since dismissed as post hoc" is fair to the re-analysis, but the report could also acknowledge that the re-analysis was right to caution against citing an unregistered seven-office correlation as a mechanism. The registered test was needed.

## Overall

This is the strongest evidence in the series. A randomised two-year result of **+8.5% to +9.8% per actual hour**, with output per employee about 3% below control, is in line with the meta-analysis's controlled estimate. It settles that the per-hour gain is neither the headline 23% nor zero.

Before publication I'd prioritise:
1. Account for the control-group meeting audit, both in estimating decay and in the meeting averages (§1).
2. Make the headline comparison like-for-like (§2).
3. Define what log hours include, and explain the meetings mechanism accordingly (§3).
4. Change "confirms" to "supports" and check clustering in the mediation (§4).
